a2-ps-s08-cp2-005: In a voluntary response sample, people choose themselves to take part.
Listeners who call in decide for themselves, and those with strong opinions are the most likely to call.
a2-ps-s08-cp2-006: A convenience sample uses whoever is easiest to reach.
People walking by the library are simply nearby, not chosen at random, and may not represent the population.
a2-ps-s08-cp1-001: An experiment imposes a treatment on the subjects; an observational study only records what happens.
The researchers assign each patient to the drug or the placebo, at random.
a2-ps-s08-cp1-002: A sample survey asks a sample of people questions and records their answers; no treatment is imposed.
Asking 500 adults about exercise collects their answers.
So this is a Sample survey.
a2-ps-s08-cp1-003: The researchers did not assign anyone to smoke or not; they only record what happened.
Recording existing traits and outcomes without imposing a treatment is an observational study.
So this is an Observational study.
a2-ps-s08-cp1-008: The margin of error is proportional to 1/√n.
Halving it needs √n to double, which means n becomes 2² = 4 times as large.
The sample size must be multiplied by 4.
a2-ps-s08-cp1-009: In an observational study, groups may differ in other ways (confounding variables) that explain the result.
Random assignment in an experiment spreads those other variables evenly between the groups.
So random assignment balances other variables between groups, leaving the treatment as the likely cause of a difference.
a2-ps-s08-honors-001: The simulation shows what differences happen by chance alone: 4.5 or more occurred 3 times in 200.
It is unlikely by chance alone (≈1.5%), so it is statistically significant.
a2-ps-s08-cp1-010: Bias is a systematic error that pushes results one way.
Voluntary response, a leading question ('Don't you agree…?') and surveying only landline owners (undercoverage) are biased.
Random selection from a full list, large random samples and random assignment are ways to avoid bias.
Bias: asking 'Don't you agree the park needs repairs?', surveying only people with landlines, and letting volunteers decide whether to respond.

A parameter is a numerical summary of a population (a statistic summarizes a sample).
